Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette:
For as long as Elena could remember, she had been the one people leaned on. At seventy-four, she still worked three days a week as a pharmacist in a small neighborhood pharmacy, her hands steady as she counted pills, her voice calm as she explained side effects to anxious patients. But that version of herself had begun to feel like a stranger, a photograph of someone she no longer recognized. The change started two years ago, when her husband of fifty years—a man she had trusted with her life—first raised his hand to her during an argument about their daughter. It had not been a single event but a series of them, escalating over months, until the night he shoved her against the kitchen counter so hard that her ribs cracked against the edge. She remembered that night not as a story with a beginning, middle, and end, but as a handful of snapshots: the sound of the door slamming as he stormed out, the cold tile against her cheek, the way her body had frozen in place as if she were already a corpse. When the memories came now, they did not arrive as a narrative. They came as those same still images, each one a photograph she could not look away from, and with them came the feeling that her body was back in that exact position—stiff, pinned, unable to move. She would be standing at the pharmacy counter, handing a customer a receipt, and suddenly her shoulders would lock, her breath would stop, and she would feel the cold floor beneath her cheek again. The shame that followed was worse than the fear. She had been a pharmacist for forty years, a mother, a grandmother, a woman who had built a life. How could she have let this happen? How could she still love the man who had done this? She had come to believe that she was weak, that she had failed some fundamental test of personhood, and that the person she used to be—capable, steady, reliable—was gone forever.

Elena had always been alert, but now her alertness had become its own kind of prison. She listened constantly. She listened for the sound of the front door opening, for the creak of a floorboard, for any noise that might mean someone was entering her home unannounced. Even when her husband was at work, even when she knew she was alone, her body remained tense, coiled, ready. She could not relax in her own living room. She could not sit down to watch television without her eyes drifting to the door, her ears straining for the click of the lock. At night, she slept on the edge of the bed, one foot on the floor, as if she might need to run. The hypervigilance had bled into her work. She began to avoid her own body—she stopped looking in mirrors, stopped noticing how her clothes fit, stopped paying attention to the ache in her ribs because acknowledging her body meant acknowledging what had happened to it. She also stopped allowing herself to feel. When a patient thanked her warmly, when a coworker touched her arm in kindness, she felt a wave of panic. Emotional closeness had become a threat. She had learned that people you loved were the ones who could hurt you, and so she began to pull away. She stopped attending family dinners. She stopped calling her daughter. She told herself it was because she was busy, but the truth was that any comment about family—even a cheerful one from a customer about their own children—sent a jolt through her chest. She avoided people altogether when she could. She took the longer route home to avoid neighbors who might want to chat. She ate dinner alone in the kitchen while her husband ate in the living room, the silence between them thick and unbroken.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was not the fear or the shame, but the loneliness. She had spent her whole life surrounded by people, and now she had almost no one. She had lost her faith—not just in her husband, but in people, in the idea that the world was safe or fair. She had lost her faith in herself. She came to the clinic because her daughter had begged her, because she could no longer bear the weight of her own silence, and because somewhere beneath the shame and the hypervigilance and the frozen snapshots of that terrible night, she still hoped that the woman she used to be might still exist. But what frightened her most was the possibility that she was right—that she was too weak to recover, that the capable Elena was gone for good, and that all that remained was a body waiting for the next door to slam.
